title: Watch hippos and wetland birds in Rusizi National Park
description: The reserve is about fifteen minutes from central Bujumbura and combines lagoons, flooded grassland and palm forest. Go with an experienced guide and treat wildlife distance as non-negotiable.

title: Hike with a ranger beneath Kibira's montane canopy
description: Kibira protects more than 40,000 hectares along the Congo-Nile divide. Access is through Busekera or Rwegura, and the tourism ministry describes ranger-led walks rather than independent entry.

title: Hear the royal drums performed at Gishora
description: The hilltop residence holds the sacred-drum sanctuary associated with Burundi's UNESCO-listed royal drum tradition. Arrange the visit rather than assuming a performance is running when you arrive.

title: Walk between the cascades of Karera Falls
description: Karera divides into six branches over three levels amid forest in southeastern Burundi. Wet rock and changing water levels make local guidance more useful than the modest walking distance suggests.

title: Follow the stream at Burundi's southern Nile source
description: A small pyramid on Mount Kikizi marks the source identified in 1934 by Burkhart Waldecker. The slight stream here is presented locally as the Nile's southernmost source.

title: Take a guided savannah walk in Ruvubu National Park
description: Burundi's largest protected ecosystem covers more than 50,000 hectares and holds buffalo, antelope, monkeys and hippos. The official tourism guidance points visitors to experienced guides for short or full-day outings.

title: Picnic above Rwegura Dam on Kibira's edge
description: Rwegura is one of Kibira's two official access points, but the dam viewpoint is a worthwhile stop in its own right. Pair it with a ranger-led forest visit and confirm current access locally.

title: Soak at Mugara's hot springs beside Kigwena Forest
description: The springs sit inside the low-elevation Kigwena Forest Reserve near Lake Tanganyika. Facilities and access conditions are lightly documented, so confirm locally before making the detour.

title: Climb the volcanic slopes of Mount Karthala
description: Karthala dominates Grande Comore and the national tourism office lists it among Ngazidja's natural sites. Use a local guide and verify volcanic and trail conditions before departure.

title: Walk Moroni's old quarter to the Friday Mosque
description: Moroni reflects the trading links between Africa, Arabia and Asia that shaped Ngazidja. Dress respectfully and treat the mosque as an active place of worship, with interior access dependent on local permission.

title: Boat among the islets of Mohéli Marine Park
description: The protected seascape is one of the national tourism office's named natural sites on Mohéli. Use a registered local boat operator and follow current park rules around reefs and wildlife.

title: Climb to Mutsamudu Citadel above the medina
description: Anjouan's capital has the archipelago's best-preserved medina, overlooked by a citadel with views across the old town. Confirm opening access locally because the tourism office gives no fixed visitor schedule.

title: Swim off Mitsamiouli's north-coast beach
description: The national tourism office lists this beach on Grande Comore's north coast. Check sea conditions on arrival and carry what you need, as services can be limited away from town.

title: Swim below Anjouan's green escarpments at Moya Beach
description: Moya is one of the beaches identified by the national tourism office on steep, volcanic Anjouan. Road and sea conditions deserve a same-day local check.

title: Hike to crater-ringed Lake Dzialandzé
description: The national tourism office identifies Dzialandzé as an Anjouan natural site, beyond the island's better-known medina and beaches. Arrange a local guide because trail detail and facilities are not published consistently.

title: Circle the rim of Lac Salé on Grande Comore
description: This small crater lake is an official Ngazidja natural-site listing near the island's northern tip. Stay on established ground around the rim and ask locally about current access.

title: Hike from Pas de Bellecombe toward Piton de la Fournaise
place: Piton de la Fournaise crater approach
description: The road reaches the Enclos viewpoint, but access farther onto the volcano changes with eruptions and official closures. Check the observatory and prefecture status before leaving.

title: Hike into roadless Cirque de Mafate
description: Mafate has no roads and its villages are reached on foot or by helicopter. Plan food and lodging ahead because even village supplies arrive mainly by air.

title: Climb Piton des Neiges from Cilaos
place: Piton des Neiges ascent from Le Bloc
description: The Le Bloc route begins inside Cirque de Cilaos and climbs to the roof of the Indian Ocean. Mountain weather changes quickly, so check trail notices and refuge availability.

title: Enter a lava tunnel with a qualified guide
description: Guided trips enter passages formed by the 2004 and 2007 flows near Sainte-Rose and Saint-Philippe. Booking is required and operators supply helmets and lights; bring long trousers and sturdy shoes.

title: Stop beneath the waterfalls of Cirque de Salazie
description: Voile de la Mariée can be seen from the road into Salazie, while reaching its lower pools needs a hike. Heavy rain feeds the falls but can also make trails unsafe.

title: Learn how Bourbon vanilla is cured at La Vanilleraie
description: The official museums-and-gardens route recommends this working vanilla stop in the north. Reserve a guided time if you want the production explanation rather than only the shop.

title: Trace indenture history at Lazaret de la Grande Chaloupe
description: The former quarantine site anchors the official western museums route and interprets settlement, slavery and indenture. Check opening days before taking the coastal detour.

title: Walk to Takamaka's forested waterfall viewpoints
description: Takamaka's trails overlook a wet, deeply cut landscape of pools and falls above Rivière des Marsouins. Rain can transform footing and river levels quickly, so use current local trail advice.

title: Walk the crater rim around Lac Dziani
description: The marked circuit takes about an hour above the turquoise crater lake. Swimming is forbidden because its alkaline water is corrosive.

title: Snorkel with green turtles off N'Gouja Beach
description: Green and hawksbill turtles use Mayotte's lagoon year-round and N'Gouja is a recognised observation beach. Keep clear of resting animals and never touch or feed them.

title: Climb Mount Choungui for a lagoon panorama
description: At 594 metres, Choungui is Mayotte's second-highest summit and overlooks the south and lagoon. The final climb is steep, so check trail conditions and use a local guide if unfamiliar with the route.

title: Boat to the white sand of the Choizil islets
description: The two undeveloped islets sit about 800 metres offshore and have no shade, food or water. Walking access exists only at low tide and the rising sea can cut off the return, making a local boat the safer choice.

title: Ride the public barge between Petite-Terre and Grande-Terre
description: The roughly fifteen-minute crossing is everyday transport for Mahorais and gives an immediate view across the island and lagoon. Check the current passenger timetable at the terminal.

title: Follow the coast into Saziley Marine Reserve
description: The southern trail rises above protected beaches and looks toward the white-sand islet offshore. Carry water and follow current reserve guidance around turtle nesting areas.

title: Paddle through Bouéni Bay's mangrove channels
description: Mayotte's best-known mangrove covers about 200 hectares and shelters nearly 28 bird species. The tourism board recommends a guide because the route mixes dry passages with kayak or pirogue sections.

title: Snorkel the clear shallows between the Choizil islets
description: Reef shelter gives the islets unusually clear water for fish and coral viewing. There are no facilities or shade, so travel with a professional and bring sun protection and drinking water.

title: Climb through cloud forest toward Pico Basilé
description: At 3,011 metres, Pico Basilé is the country's highest point and the summit can reveal Cameroon across the Gulf when cloud lifts. Confirm protected-area access and go with local guidance.

title: Step inside Malabo's twin-towered cathedral
description: The pink neo-Gothic cathedral opened in 1916 and its two towers rise about 40 metres. Respect services and confirm interior access before entering.

title: Hike to the forest waterfalls at Ureka
description: The falls lie in a Bubi sacred landscape near beaches used by nesting turtles. Visits should be locally guided so community and conservation restrictions are respected.

title: Track rainforest wildlife in Monte Alén National Park
place: Monte Alén National Park guided trek
description: The protected rainforest supports primates, antelope and exceptional birdlife. Infrastructure is limited, so arrange permits, transport and a guide before leaving Bata.

title: Boat to the beaches of Corisco Island
description: The tourism ministry promotes Corisco for its undeveloped beaches and clear water. Boat and lodging logistics require advance local arrangement rather than a spontaneous day trip.

title: Explore Annobón's volcanic island landscapes
description: Annobón combines steep green terrain, beaches and a crater-lake landscape far from the mainland. Confirm flights, local transport and accommodation before committing.

title: Visit the monumental basilica at Mongomo
place: Basilica of the Immaculate Conception Mongomo
description: The national tourism ministry identifies it as one of Africa's largest basilicas. It is an active religious site, so verify opening access and dress accordingly.

title: Watch the Río Benito flow beneath Mbini Bridge
description: The modern bridge across the Río Benito frames a quieter mainland stop with nearby beaches and local food. Treat it as a daylight detour and confirm transport back.

title: Visit a Batammariba takienta with a local guide
description: Koutammakou is a living cultural landscape, not an open-air museum. A community guide can explain how the mud tower-houses connect domestic, farming and ritual life.

title: Take the guided history tour inside Wood Home
description: The 1835 house interprets the region's clandestine slave trade through a guided visit. The tourism ministry lists the tour at about one hour; confirm current hours and price.

title: Walk down to the forest pool at Womé waterfall
description: Womé is a recognised tourism site near Kpalimé with local guides at the village. Rain changes the path and pool conditions, so follow on-site advice.

title: Explore Fazao-Malfakassa with park guidance
description: Togo's largest reserve spans roughly 2,000 square kilometres across the Fazao and Malfakassa ranges. Wildlife is not guaranteed, and access should be arranged with current park guidance.

title: Ask before photographing at Akodésséwa Fetish Market
description: This is a working centre of traditional medicine and Vodun practice. The tourism ministry explicitly tells visitors to ask before photographs and not touch objects without permission.

title: Shop for wax cloth in Lomé's Grand Marché
description: Assigamé is closely linked with the Nana Benz traders who built regional businesses around wax cloth. Keep valuables secure and ask before photographing vendors.

title: See the old ironworking furnaces at Nangbani
description: The Ministry of Tourism has identified the historic furnaces for visitor-site development. Because formal interpretation remains limited, arrange a local guide in the Bassar area.

title: Hike with local guidance to Kpètè Bèna waterfall
description: This Wawa Prefecture cascade was selected by the tourism ministry for a formal visitor-site feasibility study. Confirm current access and guide arrangements in Badou.

title: Surf the long point breaks at Robertsport
description: Liberia's tourism authority highlights Robertsport for long, consistent waves suitable for several experience levels. Arrange a local surf guide and check the day's conditions.

title: Hike with a guide in Sapo National Park
description: Sapo is Liberia's largest protected area and shelters pygmy hippos, forest elephants and chimpanzees, though sightings are never assured. Remote access and rainforest travel require advance guide and transport planning.

title: Trace Liberia's founding history on Providence Island
description: The island was the 1822 landing point for freed African-American settlers and is central to Liberia's national story. Redevelopment began in 2026, so confirm public access before visiting.

title: Swim below the first cascade at Kpatawee Falls
description: The first waterfall is close to the road; reaching the second requires about an hour's brisk hike. Use the lifeguarded area and check water conditions after heavy rain.

title: Paddle a dugout canoe on Lake Piso
description: Liberia's largest lake is a tidal lagoon rich in birdlife near Robertsport. The tourism authority says traditional canoe trips can be arranged through local guesthouses.

title: Read Liberia's history inside the National Museum
description: The museum's surviving and restored collections cover ethnic heritage, photographs, art and national history. Confirm opening hours locally because published visitor information is inconsistent.

title: Boat through the coast and wetlands around Marshall
description: The national tourism authority promotes Marshall as a day trip on the Grand Bassa coast. Arrange a licensed local operator and clarify the route before departure.

title: Hear the local history of Yeala's walls and tunnels
description: Liberia's tourism authority began work in 2026 to preserve Yeala's ancient walls, nine tunnels and oral history. Visitor infrastructure is emerging, so only go with local arrangements.

title: Meet rescued chimpanzees at Tacugama Sanctuary
description: Tacugama combines chimpanzee rehabilitation with forest conservation inside the Western Area Peninsula National Park. Book the guided visitor experience rather than arriving unannounced.

title: Walk with a guide among Tiwai Island's primates
description: The 1,200-hectare Moa River island supports 11 primate species and now forms part of Sierra Leone's first World Heritage property. Access and overnight logistics should be arranged in advance.

title: Tour the ruins of Bunce Island's slave-trade fortress
description: The island lies about 32 kilometres upriver from Freetown and preserves remains tied to the transatlantic slave trade. Boat access and interpretation are best arranged with a knowledgeable guide.

title: Cross by boat to the linked Banana Islands
description: Dublin and Ricketts islands are joined by a stone causeway, while forested and beach landscapes differ between them. The islands are reached by water, so verify transport and return timing.

title: Swim in the clear river mouth at River Number Two Beach
description: This community-managed beach is one of the National Tourism Board's headline coastal sites. Check currents where river and sea meet and use local facilities.

title: Take a guided wildlife trip in Outamba-Kilimi
description: The National Tourism Board identifies the park for hippos, chimpanzees and other wildlife. Its remoteness makes transport, guiding and current access checks essential.

title: Birdwatch with community guides in Gola Rainforest
description: Gola and Tiwai were inscribed together as Sierra Leone's first World Heritage property in 2025. Arrange the trip through current conservation and community channels.

title: Boat to the slave-trade remains on Plantain Island
description: This small Atlantic island preserves traces of its seventeenth- and eighteenth-century slave-trading role. Transport and interpretation are limited, so arrange both before leaving Freetown.
